setupSteps: Pick a stable bench and fix it. The bench must not slide. Push its far end against a wall, a power rack upright or a weight stack (RitFit advises anchoring it). A bench on a smooth floor will skid backwards when you drive up.

Check bench height. Most guides give about 14–16 in (35–40 cm) with Contreras favouring about 16 in; a standard gym flat bench is often in that range, but the exact height of your gym's bench is Not found, so test it. If your torso is long or short, adjust by foot position, not by arching.
Check the bar. Learn its weight (often 20 kg; some gyms have lighter bars) and whether the sleeves rotate.

Get a pad. Use a purpose-made bar pad if the gym has one. If not, wrap a folded yoga mat or a thick folded towel around the middle of the bar and hold it with the bar against your hips; make sure it does not slide when you lift. The bar presses hard across the hip bones and lower belly, so padding is recommended (several guides; Gravitus, Major Fitness).

Load with collars. Load equal plates on both sides, push them against the stoppers and fit collars. For heavy loads use larger plates (45 cm / 20 kg plates) so the bar sits high enough off the floor to roll easily; with small plates the bar can be hard to roll over the knees.
Start with the empty bar, or just the bench and bodyweight, for your first sessions.

Sit on the floor with your back to the bench, knees bent, with the bench about one foot (30 cm, est.) behind you. Roll the bar to sit across your hips (roll it over your legs; do not lift it on your own with a bent back). With a heavy bar, ask someone to hand it to you.

Upper-back contact. Lean back until the bottom edge of your shoulder blades rests on the bench edge. Sources vary: the bottom of the shoulder blades (StrengthLog and other guides), the middle of the shoulder blades, or just below the shoulder blades. FitPlate choice: the bench edge crosses the lower half of your shoulder blades, never your neck, never your lower back. If the bench edge is on the neck or the lower back, shuffle until it is across the blades.

Foot placement. Feet flat, about hip-width to a bit wider (sources: hip-width to shoulder-width), toes pointing straight or slightly out (about 0–30°, est.). Place them so that, at the top of the lift, your shins are vertical or nearly so (the knee roughly above the ankle). A trial of four barbell hip thrust variations (Collazo García et al., 2020) found that moving the feet further away raised hamstring activity and lowered quadriceps activity; a guide says too-near feet shorten the range, too-far feet turn it into a quad exercise.

Test the shin angle before loading. Do a bodyweight rep or two with your hands on your hips; at the top, look from the side (or ask for a photo): the shin should be near vertical. Move your feet forward or back by a foot-length (30 cm, est.) at a time until it is.

Bar on the hip crease. Place the bar (with its pad) right in the crease where the thigh meets the pelvis. Hold it with a grip just wider than your hips so the bar cannot roll up toward your belly. Do not place it on your belly.

Chin tuck and rib position. Tuck your chin gently (as if holding a small ball under it), keep your eyes on a point ahead or slightly down at the knees, and pull your ribs down toward your hips before the first rep. Contreras's guide lists forward eye gaze, chin tuck, ribs down, level torso and slight posterior pelvic tilt as the target position.

steps.title: Set the start position
steps.action: Upper back on the bench edge, feet flat, bar and pad on the hip crease, hands on the bar, chin tucked, ribs down.
steps.feel: Bar pressing evenly on the hip crease; weight carried by the feet and the bench edge on the upper back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulder blades just touching the bench edge; hips lowered to about 1–2 in (2.5–5 cm, est.) above the floor; shins vertical when the hips are at the top. Front: knees over the second toe; feet even.

steps.title: Brace and take a breath
steps.action: Take a small breath in, tighten your stomach lightly, and pull the ribs toward the hips.
steps.breathing: In through the nose; avoid a long breath-hold.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs level with the hips, not flared; chin tucked.

steps.title: Drive your hips up
steps.action: Push through the whole foot (the heels are often cued) and lift your hips until the thighs are level with the torso.
steps.feel: Buttocks squeezing hard; hamstrings working a little; no pinch in the lower back.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as the hips rise (the Valsalva breath-hold is a recognised blood-pressure risk; see Safety).
steps.visualCheck: Side: back, hips and thighs rise as one straight line from shoulder to knee; knees about 90° (est.). Front: knees stay over the toes, not caving in.

steps.title: Finish with a pause at the top
steps.action: Stop when your torso and thighs are level. Squeeze the buttocks, keep the ribs down and the chin tucked, and do not push the hips higher by arching the lower back.
steps.feel: Strong squeeze in the buttocks; lower back relaxed, not pinched.
steps.visualCheck: Side: torso roughly horizontal; shins vertical; a slight backward tilt of the pelvis (belt buckle toward the chin). Wrong: a hollow in the lower back and ribs poking up.

steps.title: Lower under control
steps.action: Let the hips travel back and down until they are about 1–2 in above the floor. Do not drop; do not touch and bounce.
steps.feel: Stretch in the buttocks and hamstrings; bar stays on the hips.
steps.breathing: Breathe in on the way down.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders stay on the bench edge; head stays still; the chin stays tucked.

steps.title: Repeat smoothly for the planned reps. Reset the ribs and chin tuck if they drift
Finish the set and put the bar down
steps.action: After the last rep, lower the hips to the floor, then roll the bar off your hips toward your feet and out over the knees (or ask a spotter to take it); set it on the floor and sit up.
steps.visualCheck: Side: you lower your hips first; you do not let the bar roll while your hips are still up.

commonMistakes.title: Arching the lower back to get "extra height"
commonMistakes.text: Arching the lower back to get "extra height". Why: the movement moves into the lumbar spine instead of the hips, takes tension off the glutes, and can irritate the back. Fix: chin tucked, ribs down, stop when thighs are level, squeeze the buttocks.

commonMistakes.title: Looking at the ceiling
commonMistakes.text: Looking at the ceiling. Why: tends to flare the ribs and push the lower back into extension. Fix: eyes on your knees or a spot ahead.

commonMistakes.title: Bench edge in the wrong place
commonMistakes.text: Bench edge in the wrong place. Why: on the neck it hurts and is unstable; on the lower back it cuts range and strains. Fix: edge across the lower half of the shoulder blades.

commonMistakes.title: Feet too far forward or too close
commonMistakes.text: Feet too far forward or too close. Why: too far out hits the hamstrings and shortens the glute range; too close turns it into a quad exercise (Collazo García 2020; coaching guides). Fix: shins vertical at the top; adjust by a foot-length.

commonMistakes.title: No bar pad
commonMistakes.text: No bar pad. Why: the bar bruises the hip bones and distracts you from lifting. Fix: pad, folded towel or mat.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the bench slide
commonMistakes.text: Letting the bench slide. Why: the bench moves and the lift becomes unstable. Fix: push the bench against a wall or rack.

commonMistakes.title: Bar sliding up to the belly or down toward the knees
commonMistakes.text: Bar sliding up to the belly or down toward the knees. Why: loses leverage and may cause the bar to roll off. Fix: bar in the hip crease, hands steady it.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing at the bottom or dropping the weight
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing at the bottom or dropping the weight. Why: loses tension and jars the spine and the bench. Fix: 2 s down, light touch, no bounce.

commonMistakes.title: Loading too heavy too soon
commonMistakes.text: Loading too heavy too soon. Why: form breaks (arching, short range, hips twisting). Fix: empty bar until 3 x 10 are smooth; Contreras says stop a heavy set when you can no longer hold your spine and pelvis position.

commonMistakes.title: Knees caving in
commonMistakes.text: Knees caving in. Why: strains the knee and shifts load. Fix: push knees out over toes; lighter weight.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath on every rep
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath on every rep. Why: raises blood pressure (see Safety). Fix: breathe out as the hips rise.

safetyNotes: Back problems: keep the ribs down and avoid arching; start with a glute bridge. Hip thrust-specific evidence for people with back pain: Not found; ask a professional.
Knee problems: the knees stay bent about 90° with little extra knee load; reduce the load if the front of the knee hurts.
Hip or groin problems: the bar presses on the hip crease; pad well and reduce load if the hip bones or the pubic area hurt.

High blood pressure: the breath-hold (Valsalva manoeuvre) raises intra-abdominal pressure and blood pressure. A 2013 systematic review found it raises blood pressure during resistance exercise but its health risks remain unconfirmed. Breathe out on each lift, avoid sets to failure, and keep loads moderate. Do not lift when resting BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis: see the table; ask a professional. Lying-back positions and a heavy bar over the belly are a problem in later pregnancy; ask your obstetrician.
Men and women: the bar presses on the hip bones and pelvic area; pad well and keep the bar on the hip crease (several guides).
